rows.text: For most of my adult life, freedom meant that no one could tell me what to do with my time.
I had spent my childhood trying to meet other people’s expectations, and years working at a job I wanted to leave.
When I finally retired at 31, I loved waking up knowing the day belonged to me.
That’s one reason I was afraid to have a child.
I knew what it would mean to have someone need me every day.
I worried that after working so hard to get my time back, I would give it all away.
Then my father-in-law said something I didn’t expect.
He told Bryce and I that he hoped we’d have a child, but if we never did, he would love us just the same.
He wanted a grandchild, but he didn’t make his love depend on one.
Somehow, being given room to say no made it easier for me to imagine saying yes.
Years later, he was diagnosed with brain cancer.
During his final month of life, I was nine months pregnant.
Our days filled with family calls and care he could no longer manage alone.
I watched his daughter gently trim his nails.
I watched my husband help him with things a grown man would rather never need help with.
And friends and family kept coming just to sit beside him.
By then, he had nothing left to offer them.
He had spent years loving people without asking them to earn it, and now they wanted to be there.
Watching them, I understood something I hadn’t understood when I was younger: being needed by someone you love can feel very different from being trapped.
Now I have a son who needs lunch made, a story read again, and someone willing to stop and look at a bug with him.
I still miss the ease of leaving whenever I want.
But when he runs to me at daycare, I think about his grandfather.
I want my son to feel the same freedom he gave us: to know that I love him without asking him to repay me.
Money gave me the freedom to choose how to spend my time.
My father-in-law helped me see why I might choose to give some of it away.
